$$ \pro\colon{\mathbb{S}}/G_{0}\to{\mathbb{S}}/({\mathbb{G}}_{m}\ltimes G_{0}). $$

Let $\pro_{{\mathbb{S}}/{\mathbb{G}}_{m}},\chi\colon({\mathbb{S}}/G_{0})\times{\mathbb{G}}_{m}\to{\mathbb{S}}/G_{0}$ be the projection and the action morphisms respectively. We have to construct an equivalence

$$ \pro_{{\mathbb{S}}/{\mathbb{G}}_{m}}^{*}(({\mathcal{A}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\operatorname{\mathsf{-Mod}}})_{{\mathbb{S}}/G_{0}})\mathrel{\mathop{\kern 0.0pt\longrightarrow}\limits^{\sim}}\chi^{*}(({\mathcal{A}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\operatorname{\mathsf{-Mod}}})_{{\mathbb{S}}/G_{0}}) $$

together with the cocycle datum. Note the ${\mathbb{G}}_{m}$ -equivariant structure on ${\mathcal{A}}_{\mathbb{S}}$ identifies the pullback of the quasi-coherent sheaves in question to ${\mathbb{S}}\times{\mathbb{G}}_{m}$ with ${\mathcal{A}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\operatorname{\mathsf{-Mod}}}$ lifted along $\pro_{\mathbb{S}}\colon{\mathbb{S}}\times{\mathbb{G}}_{m}\to{\mathbb{S}}$ . Thus, each quasi-coherent sheaf of categories determines an action of $G_{0}$ on $\pro_{\mathbb{S}}^{*}{\mathcal{A}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\operatorname{\mathsf{-Mod}}}$ each of which comes with a trivialization over $\infty\times{\mathbb{G}}_{m}$ . Using Remark 5.3 there exists a unique isomorphism between the two actions compatible with trivializations. This gives equivalence (5.15). Construction of the cocycle datum is left to the reader.

For uniqueness assertion, observe that if $(({\mathcal{A}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\operatorname{\mathsf{-Mod}}})_{{\mathbb{S}}/({\mathbb{G}}_{m}\ltimes G_{0})},\Theta,\Xi_{\infty},\varpi)$ is a quadruple from the Proposition, then, by Theorem 1, $\pro^{*}(({\mathcal{A}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\operatorname{\mathsf{-Mod}}})_{{\mathbb{S}}/({\mathbb{G}}_{m}\ltimes G_{0})})$ is equivalent to $({\mathcal{A}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\operatorname{\mathsf{-Mod}}})_{{\mathbb{S}}/G_{0}}$ . Hence $({\mathcal{A}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\operatorname{\mathsf{-Mod}}})_{{\mathbb{S}}/({\mathbb{G}}_{m}\ltimes G_{0})}$ arises from a descent data along $\pro_{\mathbb{S}}$ as above and our assertion also follows from “up to a unique isomorphism” part of Remark 5.3.

As in §5.2 to prove the last assertion of the Proposition it suffices to construct a ${\mathbb{G}}_{m}$ -invariant section $G_{0}\times 0\to\widehat{G}_{\mathbb{S}}\times_{\mathbb{S}}0$ . In fact, the uniqueness of $\widehat{\tau}$ in (5.10) implies that the latter is ${\mathbb{G}}_{m}$ -equivariant. It follows that the same is true for section (5.11). ∎

### 5.4. Further remarks.

The following corollary of Theorem 1 will be used in §6.4.

#### Proposition 5.8.

Let $f\colon T\to G_{0}\times{\mathbb{S}}$ be a morphism of schemes, $T_{0}\hookrightarrow T$ the scheme theoretic fiber of $f$ over $G_{0}\times 0$ . Then Zariski locally on $T$ there exists a morphism $g\colon T\to\underline{\Aut}({\mathcal{A}}_{\mathbb{S}})$ such that $f_{|T_{0}}=g_{|T_{0}}$ .

#### Proof.

Consider the action of $G_{0}$ on ${\mathcal{A}}_{S}{\operatorname{\mathsf{-Mod}}}$ from Theorem 1 and let

$$ 1\to\underline{{\mathcal{A}}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{*}\to\widehat{G}_{\mathbb{S}}\to G_{0}\times{\mathbb{S}}\to 1 $$

be the extension corresponding to this action by Remark 5.1. As explained in loc. cit. Zariski locally on $T$ the map $f$ admits a lifting $\tilde{f}\colon T\to\widehat{G}_{\mathbb{S}}$ . The composition of $\tilde{f}$ with $\alpha\colon\widehat{G}_{\mathbb{S}}\to\underline{\Aut}({\mathcal{A}}_{\mathbb{S}})$ does the job. ∎

#### Remark 5.9.

We claim that the action of $G_{0}$ on ${\mathcal{A}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\operatorname{\mathsf{-Mod}}}$ constructed above does not lift to an action on the algebra ${\mathcal{A}}_{\mathbb{S}}$ even if ${\mathbb{S}}$ is replaced by the formal completion $\hat{\mathbb{S}}$ . To see this we shall prove that the surjection $r\colon G=\underline{\Aut}(A_{h})\twoheadrightarrow G_{0}$ has no sections i.e., group homomorphisms $s\colon G_{0}\to G$ with $r\circ s=\Id$ . Assuming the contrary consider the induced morphisms of the restricted Lie algebras. Write $k={\mathbb{F}}_{p}$ . The restricted Lie algebra $\Lie G_{0}$ is the algebra of Hamiltonian vector fields on $\Spec A_{0}$ ([BK, Lemma 3.3.]). It follows that $\Lie G$ , the restricted Lie algebra of $k[[h]]$ -linear derivations of the associative algebra $A_{h}$ , can be identified with the Lie subalgebra $\frac{1}{h}(A_{h}/k[[h]])\subset A_{h}(h^{-1})/k((h))$ :

$$ 0\to\tfrac{1}{h}k[[h]]\to\tfrac{1}{h}A_{h}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\ad}}{{\longrightarrow}}\operatorname{Der}A_{h}\to 0. $$

In particular, $\Lie G$ has the structure of restricted Lie algebra over $k[[h]]$ and the differential of $r$ is identified with projection

$$ dr\colon\Lie G\to\Lie G/h\Lie G=\Lie G_{0}. $$

Thus, $ds$ defines an isomorphism of restricted Lie algebras over $k[[h]]$

$$ \Lie G_{0}\otimes_{k}k[[h]]\mathrel{\mathop{\kern 0.0pt\longrightarrow}\limits^{\sim}}\Lie G. $$

Consequently, we have $\Lie G_{0}\otimes_{k}k((h))\mathrel{\mathop{\kern 0.0pt\longrightarrow}\limits^{\sim}}\Lie G\otimes_{k[[h]]}k((h))$ . The isomorphism $A_{h}(h^{-1})=\Mat_{p^{n}}(k((h)))$ identifies $\Lie G\otimes_{k[[h]]}k((h))$ with $\mathfrak{pgl}_{p^{n}}(\,k((h))\,)$ , the quotient of $\mathfrak{gl}_{p^{n}}(\,k((h))\,)$ by its center. It is shown in [BV, Lemma 4.4] that there exists a split surjection $G_{0}\to{\mathbb{G}}_{a}$ . This yields a nonzero homomorphism of restricted Lie algebras $\Lie G_{0}\otimes_{k}k((h))\to k((h))$ , where $k((h))$ is equipped with the zero $p$ -th power operation. We claim that $\mathfrak{pgl}_{p^{n}}(k((h)))$ does not admit such homomorphisms. Indeed, the quotient $\mathfrak{gl}/[\mathfrak{gl},\mathfrak{gl}]$ is the restricted Lie algebra of the multiplicative group. In particular, $p$ -th power operation on this quotient is non-trivial. This contradiction completes the proof.

## 6. Canonical quantization of $\QCoh(X)$ .

### 6.1. Construction of the canonical quantization and its uniqueness.

For the duration of this subsection let $S$ be a scheme over ${\mathbb{F}}_{p}$ with $p>2$ , and let $(X,[\eta])$ be a quasi-smooth scheme over $S$ equipped a restricted symplectic structure

$$ [\eta]\in H^{0}(X,\coker({\mathcal{O}}_{X}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\longrightarrow}}\Omega^{1}_{X/S})). $$

We shall also assume that the rank of the vector bundle $\Omega^{1}_{X/S}$ is constant, say, $2n$ , for some $n\in{\mathbb{Z}}$ . In particular, $d[\eta]=:\omega$ is a symplectic form on $X/S$ meaning that $\wedge^{n}\omega$ does not vanish. Let $\pi\colon{\mathcal{M}}_{X,[\eta]}\to X^{\{\!\!\!\ p\ \!\!\!\}}$ be the $G_{0}$ -torsor of Darboux frames (see Construction 2.68). Denote by $\xi\colon X^{\{\!\!\!\ p\ \!\!\!\}}\to BG_{0}$ the morphism corresponding to the latter. In Theorem 1 we constructed an action of $G_{0}$ on ${\mathcal{A}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\operatorname{\mathsf{-Mod}}}$ and the corresponding quasi-coherent sheaf of categories $({\mathcal{A}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\operatorname{\mathsf{-Mod}}})_{{\mathbb{S}}/G_{0}}$ on ${\mathbb{S}}/G_{0}$ . Let $\QCoh_{h}$ be its pullback via the morphism $\xi\times\Id\colon X^{\{\!\!\!\ p\ \!\!\!\}}\times{\mathbb{S}}\to BG_{0}\times{\mathbb{S}}={\mathbb{S}}/G_{0}$ . The sheaf of categories $\QCoh_{h}$ is equipped with the following pieces of structure

- (i) An equivalences $\Theta\colon(\pi\times\Id)^{*}\QCoh_{h}\mathrel{\mathop{\kern 0.0pt\longrightarrow}\limits^{\sim}}\pro_{\mathbb{S}}^{*}{\mathcal{A}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\operatorname{\mathsf{-Mod}}}$ of quasi-coherent sheaves of categories over ${\mathcal{M}}_{X,[\eta]}\times{\mathbb{S}}$ . Here $\pro_{\mathbb{S}}\colon{\mathcal{M}}_{X,[\eta]}\times{\mathbb{S}}\to{\mathbb{S}}$ is the projection.

- (ii) An equivalences $\Xi_{\infty}\colon(\QCoh_{h})_{|X^{\{\!\!\!\ p\ \!\!\!\}}\times\{\infty\}}\mathrel{\mathop{\kern 0.0pt\longrightarrow}\limits^{\sim}}{\mathcal{O}}_{X^{\{\!\!\!\ p\ \!\!\!\}}}{\operatorname{\mathsf{-Mod}}}$ of quasi-coherent sheaves of categories over $X^{\{\!\!\!\ p\ \!\!\!\}}$ together with an isomorphism $\varpi$ between the pullback of $\Xi_{\infty}$ to ${\mathcal{M}}_{X,[\eta]}$ and the restriction of $\Theta$ to ${\mathcal{M}}_{X,[\eta]}\times\{\infty\}$ 2727 27 The restriction of $\Theta$ yields $\pi^{*}(\QCoh_{h})_{|X^{\{\!\!\!\ p\ \!\!\!\}}\times\{\infty\}}\mathrel{\mathop{\kern 0.0pt\longrightarrow}\limits^{\sim}}(\pro_{\mathbb{S}}^{*}{\mathcal{A}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\operatorname{\mathsf{-Mod}}})_{|{\mathcal{M}}_{X,[\eta]}\times\{\infty\}}\mathrel{\mathop{\kern 0.0pt\longrightarrow}\limits^{\sim}}{\mathcal{O}}_{{\mathcal{M}}_{X,[\eta]}}{\operatorname{\mathsf{-Mod}}}$ , where the second equivalence comes from (3.17)..

and enjoys the following property

- (P) The isomorphism $\Center(\pi^{*}((\QCoh_{h})_{|X^{\{\!\!\!\ p\ \!\!\!\}}\times\{0\}}))\simeq\pro^{*}A_{0}$ descends to $\Center((\QCoh_{h})_{|X^{\{\!\!\!\ p\ \!\!\!\}}\times\{0\}})\simeq F_{*}{\mathcal{O}}_{X}$ , where $F\colon X\to X^{\{\!\!\!\ p\ \!\!\!\}}$ is the relative Frobenius morphism.

Part (i) comes from the construction of $\QCoh_{h}$ as a decent of $\pro_{\mathbb{S}}^{*}{\mathcal{A}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\operatorname{\mathsf{-Mod}}}$ along ${\mathcal{M}}_{X,[\eta]}\times{\mathbb{S}}\to X^{\{\!\!\!\ p\ \!\!\!\}}\times{\mathbb{S}}$ . Part (ii) is induced by the trivialization of the $G_{0}$ -action on the fiber of ${\mathcal{A}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\operatorname{\mathsf{-Mod}}}$ at $h=\infty$ . Lastly, property (P) is derived from the isomorphism $F_{*}{\mathcal{O}}_{X}\simeq{\mathcal{M}}_{X,[\eta]}\times^{G_{0}}A_{0}$ , where $A_{0}$ is equipped with the tautological action of $G_{0}$ . We shall refer to the quadruple $(\QCoh_{h},\Theta,\Xi_{\infty},\varpi)$ as the canonical quantization of $\QCoh(X)$ .

#### Proposition 6.1.

The quadruple $(\QCoh_{h},\Theta,\Xi_{\infty},\varpi)$ is uniquely characterized by property (P).

#### Proof.

Let $({\mathfrak{S}}_{i},\Theta_{i},\Xi_{\infty,i},\varpi_{i})$ , $i=1,2$ , be quadruples with property (P). We shall prove that there exists a unique equivalence (up to a unique isomorphism) connecting the two. The argument is similar to the proof of the uniqueness part of Theorem 1. Giving a pair $({\mathfrak{S}}_{i},\Theta_{i})$ is equivalent equivalent to specifying the descent data for $\pro_{\mathbb{S}}^{*}{\mathcal{A}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\operatorname{\mathsf{-Mod}}}$ along the morphism ${\mathcal{M}}_{X,[\eta]}\times{\mathbb{S}}\to{\mathcal{M}}_{X,[\eta]}/G_{0}\times{\mathbb{S}}=X^{\{\!\!\!\ p\ \!\!\!\}}\times{\mathbb{S}}$ . In particular, $({\mathfrak{S}}_{i},\Theta_{i})$ determines an autoequivalence $\phi_{i}$ of ${\mathcal{A}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\operatorname{\mathsf{-Mod}}}$ lifted to $G_{0}\times{\mathcal{M}}_{X,[\eta]}\times{\mathbb{S}}$ . Property (P) implies that the composition $\phi_{1}\otimes\phi_{2}^{-1}$ acts as $\Id$ on the center of ${\mathcal{A}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\operatorname{\mathsf{-Mod}}}$ pulled back to $G_{0}\times{\mathcal{M}}_{X,[\eta]}\times\{0\}$ . Applying Lemma 5.2 we conclude that $\phi_{1}\otimes\phi_{2}^{-1}$ is the tensor product with a line bundle $L$ over $G_{0}\times{\mathcal{M}}_{X,[\eta]}\times{\mathbb{S}}$ . The equivalence $\Xi_{\infty,i}$ yields an isomorphism between $\phi_{i}$ restricted to $G_{0}\times{\mathcal{M}}_{X,[\eta]}\times\{\infty\}$ and the identity functor. In turn, the latter determines a trivialization of $L$ restricted to $G_{0}\times{\mathcal{M}}_{X,[\eta]}\times\infty$ . The groupoid of line bundles over $G_{0}\times{\mathcal{M}}_{X,[\eta]}\times{\mathbb{S}}$ equipped with a trivialization over $G_{0}\times{\mathcal{M}}_{X,[\eta]}\times\{\infty\}$ is discrete and its $\pi_{0}$ is the group $H^{0}(G_{0}\times{\mathcal{M}}_{X,[\eta]},{\mathbb{Z}})={\mathbb{Z}}$ . Finally, the cocycle constraint implies that $\phi_{i}$ and, hence, $\phi_{1}\otimes\phi_{2}^{-1}$ is isomorphic to $\Id$ when restricted to $1_{G_{0}}\times{\mathcal{M}}_{X,[\eta]}\times\{\infty\}$ . This defines a trivialization of $L$ . ∎

By property (P) $(\QCoh_{h})_{|X^{\{\!\!\!\ p\ \!\!\!\}}\times\{0\}}$ has a $F_{*}{\mathcal{O}}_{X}$ -linear structure. Moreover, by (i), locally for the fpqc topology, $(\QCoh_{h})_{|X^{\{\!\!\!\ p\ \!\!\!\}}\times\{0\}}$ , as a quasi-coherent sheaf of categories with a $F_{*}{\mathcal{O}}_{X}$ -linear structure, is equivalent to $F_{*}{\mathcal{O}}_{X}{\operatorname{\mathsf{-Mod}}}$ . We shall see that this also holds globally. To this end, observe that, for any ring $A$ , the groupoid of autoequivalences of $A{\operatorname{\mathsf{-Mod}}}$ is identified with the groupoid of autoequivalences of $A^{op}{\operatorname{\mathsf{-Mod}}}$ . In particular, the descent data for $\pro_{\mathbb{S}}^{*}{\mathcal{A}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\operatorname{\mathsf{-Mod}}}$ along the morphism ${\mathcal{M}}_{X,[\eta]}\times{\mathbb{S}}\to X^{\{\!\!\!\ p\ \!\!\!\}}\times{\mathbb{S}}$ specified by $(\QCoh_{h},\Theta)$ determines a descent data for $\pro_{\mathbb{S}}^{*}{\mathcal{A}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{op}{\operatorname{\mathsf{-Mod}}}$ . We denote $\QCoh_{h}^{\circ}$ the corresponding sheaf of categories over $X^{\{\!\!\!\ p\ \!\!\!\}}\times{\mathbb{S}}$ and by $\Theta^{\circ}\colon(\pi\times\Id)^{*}\QCoh_{h}^{\circ}\mathrel{\mathop{\kern 0.0pt\longrightarrow}\limits^{\sim}}\pro_{\mathbb{S}}^{*}{\mathcal{A}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{op}{\operatorname{\mathsf{-Mod}}}$ the equivalence it comes with. Explicitly, $\QCoh_{h}^{\circ}$ assigns to each $Z\stackrel{{\scriptstyle u}}{{\longrightarrow}}X^{\{\!\!\!\ p\ \!\!\!\}}\times{\mathbb{S}}$ the category of all right exact ${\mathcal{O}}$ -linear functors $u^{*}\QCoh_{h}\to{\mathcal{O}}_{Z}{\operatorname{\mathsf{-Mod}}}$ that commute with all direct sums2828 28 To see this observe that, for any ring $A$ , the category of right $A$ -modules is equivalent to the category of right exact functors from left $A$ -modules to abelian groups that commute with all direct sums.. Equivalence $\Xi_{\infty}$ and isomorphism $\varpi$ determine $\Xi^{\circ}_{\infty}\colon(\QCoh_{h}^{\circ})_{|X^{\{\!\!\!\ p\ \!\!\!\}}\times\{\infty\}}\mathrel{\mathop{\kern 0.0pt\longrightarrow}\limits^{\sim}}{\mathcal{O}}_{X^{\{\!\!\!\ p\ \!\!\!\}}}{\operatorname{\mathsf{-Mod}}}$ , $\varpi^{\circ}$ . Next, recall from (5.9) an isomorphism $\alpha\colon\iota^{*}{\mathcal{A}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{op}\mathrel{\mathop{\kern 0.0pt\longrightarrow}\limits^{\sim}}{\mathcal{A}}_{\mathbb{S}}$ . By Proposition 6.1 there exists a unique equivalence of the triples

$$ \Sigma\colon(\QCoh_{h},\Theta,\Xi_{\infty},\varpi)\mathrel{\mathop{\kern 0.0pt\longrightarrow}\limits^{\sim}}(({\Id}\times\iota)^{*}\QCoh_{h}^{\circ},\alpha\circ\Theta^{\circ},\Xi^{\circ}_{\infty},\varpi^{\circ}). $$

Denote by

$$ \Sigma_{0}\colon(\QCoh_{h})_{|X^{\{\!\!\!\ p\ \!\!\!\}}\times\{0\}}\mathrel{\mathop{\kern 0.0pt\longrightarrow}\limits^{\sim}}(\QCoh_{h}^{\circ})_{|X^{\{\!\!\!\ p\ \!\!\!\}}\times\{0\}} $$

the restriction of the latter to $X^{\{\!\!\!\ p\ \!\!\!\}}\times\{0\}$ . Observe that the pullback $\Sigma_{0}$ to ${\mathcal{M}}_{X,[\eta]}\times\{0\}$ is naturally isomorphic to the identity functor $\pro^{*}A_{0}{\operatorname{\mathsf{-Mod}}}\simeq\pro^{*}{A_{0}^{op}}{\operatorname{\mathsf{-Mod}}}$ . Every $F_{*}{\mathcal{O}}_{X}$ -linear equivalence $\Xi_{0}\colon(\QCoh_{h})_{|X^{\{\!\!\!\ p\ \!\!\!\}}\times\{0\}}\mathrel{\mathop{\kern 0.0pt\longrightarrow}\limits^{\sim}}F_{*}{\mathcal{O}}_{X}{\operatorname{\mathsf{-Mod}}}$ induces $(\QCoh_{h}^{\circ})_{|X^{\{\!\!\!\ p\ \!\!\!\}}\times\{0\}}\mathrel{\mathop{\kern 0.0pt\longrightarrow}\limits^{\sim}}F_{*}{\mathcal{O}}_{X}{\operatorname{\mathsf{-Mod}}}$ denoted by $\Xi_{0}^{\circ}$ .

#### Proposition 6.2.

There exists a unique triple $(\Xi_{0},\kappa,\upsilon)$ , where

$$ \Xi_{0}\colon(\QCoh_{h})_{|X^{\{\!\!\!\ p\ \!\!\!\}}\times\{0\}}\mathrel{\mathop{\kern 0.0pt\longrightarrow}\limits^{\sim}}F_{*}{\mathcal{O}}_{X}{\operatorname{\mathsf{-Mod}}} $$

is a $F_{*}{\mathcal{O}}_{X}$ -linear equivalence of quasi-coherent sheaves of categories over $X^{\{\!\!\!\ p\ \!\!\!\}}$ , $\kappa$ is an isomorphism between $\pi^{*}(\Xi_{0})$ and the composite

$$ \pi^{*}((\QCoh_{h})_{|X^{\{\!\!\!\ p\ \!\!\!\}}\times\{0\}})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\Theta}}{{\mathrel{\mathop{\kern 0.0pt\longrightarrow}\limits^{\sim}}}}\pro^{*}A_{0}{\operatorname{\mathsf{-Mod}}}\mathrel{\mathop{\kern 0.0pt\longrightarrow}\limits^{\sim}}\pi^{*}(F_{*}{\mathcal{O}}_{X}){\operatorname{\mathsf{-Mod}}}\mathrel{\mathop{\kern 0.0pt\longrightarrow}\limits^{\sim}}\pi^{*}(F_{*}{\mathcal{O}}_{X}{\operatorname{\mathsf{-Mod}}}), $$

and $\upsilon$ is an isomorphism $\Xi_{0}^{\circ}\circ\Sigma_{0}\mathrel{\mathop{\kern 0.0pt\longrightarrow}\limits^{\sim}}\Xi_{0}$ compatible with $\kappa$ .

#### Proof.

Locally, for the fpqc topology, $(\QCoh_{h})_{|X^{\{\!\!\!\ p\ \!\!\!\}}\times\{0\}}$ , as a quasi-coherent sheaf of categories with a $F_{*}{\mathcal{O}}_{X}$ -linear structure, is equivalent, to $F_{*}{\mathcal{O}}_{X}{\operatorname{\mathsf{-Mod}}}$ . Assigning to a scheme over $X^{\{\!\!\!\ p\ \!\!\!\}}$ the groupoid of such equivalences we define a gerbe on $X^{\{\!\!\!\ p\ \!\!\!\}}$ banded by the group scheme of invertible elements in $F_{*}{\mathcal{O}}_{X}$ or, equivalently, a gerbe ${\mathcal{E}}$ on $X$ banded by ${\mathbb{G}}_{m}$ . The equivalence $\Sigma_{0}$ amounts to specifying an isomorphism between ${\mathcal{E}}$ and the opposite gerbe i.e., the reduction of ${\mathcal{E}}$ to a gerbe ${\mathcal{E}}^{\prime}$ on $X$ banded by $\mu_{2}\subset{\mathbb{G}}_{m}$ . By construction the pullback of ${\mathcal{E}}^{\prime}$ to ${\mathcal{M}}_{X,[\eta]}\times_{X^{\{\!\!\!\ p\ \!\!\!\}}}X$ is trivialized. To prove Proposition 6.2 it suffices to show that every $\mu_{2}$ -gerbe on $X$ equipped with a trivialization over ${\mathcal{M}}_{X,[\eta]}\times_{X^{\{\!\!\!\ p\ \!\!\!\}}}X$ admits a unique trivialization (compatible with the given trivialization over ${\mathcal{M}}_{X,[\eta]}\times_{X^{\{\!\!\!\ p\ \!\!\!\}}}X$ ). In the latter, amounts to showing that the pullback map

$$ H^{i}_{et}(X,\mu_{2})\to H^{i}_{et}({\mathcal{M}}_{X,[\eta]}\times_{X^{\{\!\!\!\ p\ \!\!\!\}}}X,\mu_{2}) $$

is an isomorphism $i=0,1$ and injective for $i=2$ . The morphism $\pi\times\Id\colon{\mathcal{M}}_{X,[\eta]}\times_{X^{\{\!\!\!\ p\ \!\!\!\}}}X\to X$ is a $G_{0}$ -torsor locally trivial for the étale topology. Hence, using the vanishing of $H^{i}_{et}(G_{0},\mu_{2})$ , for $i=0,1$ , we conclude that $\mu_{2}\mathrel{\mathop{\kern 0.0pt\longrightarrow}\limits^{\sim}}\tau_{<2}R(\pi\times\Id)_{*}\mu_{2}$ . This implies the claim. ∎

#### Remark 6.3.

Here is another construction of $(\Xi_{0},\kappa,\upsilon)$ . Section (5.11) defines a lift of the $G_{0}$ -torsor ${\mathcal{M}}_{X,[\eta]}\to X^{\{\!\!\!\ p\ \!\!\!\}}$ to a $\hat{G}_{\mathbb{S}}\times_{\mathbb{S}}\{0\}$ -torsor. Now (6.1) comes from the equivalence in Proposition 4.3 and the isomorphism $F_{*}{\mathcal{O}}_{X}\simeq{\mathcal{M}}_{X,[\eta]}\times^{G_{0}}A_{0}$ . We leave it the reader to produce $\kappa$ and $\upsilon$ .

Observe that (6.1) yields, in particular, an equivalence between the category $\QCoh_{h}(X^{\{\!\!\!\ p\ \!\!\!\}}\times\{0\})$ and the category of quasi-coherent sheaves on $X$ .

### 6.2. ${\mathbb{G}}_{m}$ -equivariant quantizations.

Let $S$ be a scheme over ${\mathbb{F}}_{p}$ with $p>2$ , and let $(X,\omega)$ be a scheme quasi-smooth over $S$ equipped with a symplectic $2$ -form $\omega\in\Omega^{2}_{X/S}(X)$ and a ${\mathbb{G}}_{m}$ -action

$$ \gamma\colon{\mathbb{G}}_{m}\times X\to X. $$

We assume that $\gamma$ is a morphism of schemes over $S$ and the following identity holds

$$ \gamma^{*}\omega=z^{m}\proj_{X}^{*}\omega, $$

for some integer $m$ invertible in ${\mathbb{F}}_{p}$ . Here $z$ denotes the coordinate on ${\mathbb{G}}_{m}$ and $\proj_{X}\colon{\mathbb{G}}_{m}\times X\to X$ the projection. The ${\mathbb{G}}_{m}$ -action on $X$ defines a homomorphism from the Lie algebra of ${\mathbb{G}}_{m}$ to the Lie algebra of vector fields on $X$ . Denote by $\theta$ the image of the generator $z\frac{\partial}{\partial z}$ of $\Lie{\mathbb{G}}_{m}$ . Formula (6.3) together with the identity $d\omega=0$ imply that

$$ d\iota_{\theta}\omega=m\omega. $$

Hence, $1$ -form $\eta=\frac{1}{m}\iota_{\theta}\omega$ , defines a restricted Poisson structure on $X$ . Observe that the composition

$$ {\mathbb{G}}_{m}\times{X^{(1)}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle F_{{\mathbb{G}}_{m}}\times\Id}}{{\longrightarrow}}{\mathbb{G}}_{m}\times{X^{(1)}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\gamma^{\prime}}}{{\longrightarrow}}{X^{(1)}}, $$

where $F_{{\mathbb{G}}_{m}}$ is the Frobenius morphism on ${\mathbb{G}}_{m}$ , carries the closed subscheme ${\mathbb{G}}_{m}\times X^{\{\!\!\!\ p\ \!\!\!\}}\hookrightarrow{\mathbb{G}}_{m}\times{X^{(1)}}$ to $X^{\{\!\!\!\ p\ \!\!\!\}}\hookrightarrow{X^{(1)}}$ yielding a morphism

$$ \gamma_{p}\colon{\mathbb{G}}_{m}\times X^{\{\!\!\!\ p\ \!\!\!\}}\to X^{\{\!\!\!\ p\ \!\!\!\}}. $$

Endow $X^{\{\!\!\!\ p\ \!\!\!\}}$ with a ${\mathbb{G}}_{m}$ -action given by $\gamma_{p}$ . Note that the Frobenius morphism $F\colon X\to X^{\{\!\!\!\ p\ \!\!\!\}}$ is ${\mathbb{G}}_{m}$ -equivariant. Also, consider the action $\chi_{m}\colon{\mathbb{G}}_{m}\times{\mathbb{S}}\to{\mathbb{S}}$ given by the formula $\chi_{m}^{*}(h)=z^{m}h$ . We shall see that the canonical quantization $\QCoh_{h}$ comes equipped with a ${\mathbb{G}}_{m}$ -equivariant structure with respect to the diagonal action $(\gamma_{p},\chi_{m})\colon{\mathbb{G}}_{m}\times(X^{\{\!\!\!\ p\ \!\!\!\}}\times{\mathbb{S}})\to X^{\{\!\!\!\ p\ \!\!\!\}}\times{\mathbb{S}}$ . Let us explain a construction of the corresponding quasi-coherent sheaf of categories $(\QCoh_{h})_{(X^{\{\!\!\!\ p\ \!\!\!\}}\times{\mathbb{S}})/_{\!\gamma_{p},\chi_{m}}{\mathbb{G}}_{m}}$ on the quotient stack $(X^{\{\!\!\!\ p\ \!\!\!\}}\times{\mathbb{S}})/_{\!\gamma_{p},\chi_{m}}{\mathbb{G}}_{m}$ .

Recall from §5.3 the homomorphism $\lambda\colon{\mathbb{G}}_{m}\to\Aut(A_{0})$ and denote by $\lambda_{m}$ its pre-composition with the isogeny $t_{m}\colon{\mathbb{G}}_{m}\to{\mathbb{G}}_{m}$ , $t^{*}_{m}(z)=z^{m}$ . The action of ${\mathbb{G}}_{m}$ on $A_{0}$ normalizes $G_{0}\subset\Aut(A_{0})$ . Denote by ${\mathbb{G}}_{m}\ltimes_{\Ad_{\lambda_{m}}}G_{0}$ the corresponding semidirect product. Let $\pi\colon{\mathcal{M}}_{X,[\eta]}\to{X^{\{\!\!\!\ p\ \!\!\!\}}}$ be the $G_{0}$ -torsor of Darboux frames. Then, using $\lambda_{m}$ and $\gamma$ , the action of $G_{0}$ on ${\mathcal{M}}_{X,[\eta]}$ extends to an action of ${\mathbb{G}}_{m}\ltimes_{\Ad_{\lambda_{m}}}G_{0}$ making $\pi$ equivariant with respect to this larger group. The product ${\mathcal{M}}_{X,[\eta]}\times{\mathbb{S}}$ equipped with diagonal action of ${\mathbb{G}}_{m}\ltimes_{\Ad_{\lambda_{m}}}G_{0}$ yields a morphism of stacks

$$ (X^{\{\!\!\!\ p\ \!\!\!\}}\times{\mathbb{S}})/_{\!\gamma_{p},\chi_{m}}{\mathbb{G}}_{m}\mathrel{\mathop{\kern 0.0pt\longrightarrow}\limits^{\sim}}({\mathcal{M}}_{X,[\eta]}\times{\mathbb{S}})/({\mathbb{G}}_{m}\ltimes_{\Ad_{\lambda_{m}}}G_{0})\to{\mathbb{S}}/_{\!\chi_{m}}({\mathbb{G}}_{m}\ltimes_{\Ad_{\lambda_{m}}}G_{0}) $$

The homomorphism

$$ {\mathbb{G}}_{m}\ltimes_{\Ad_{\lambda_{m}}}G_{0}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle t_{m}\times\Id}}{{\longrightarrow}}{\mathbb{G}}_{m}\ltimes_{\Ad_{\lambda}}G_{0} $$

and the identity map on ${\mathbb{S}}$ induce a morphism

$$ S/_{\!\chi_{m}}({\mathbb{G}}_{m}\ltimes_{\Ad_{\lambda_{m}}}G_{0})\to{\mathbb{S}}/_{\!\chi}({\mathbb{G}}_{m}\ltimes_{\Ad_{\lambda}}G_{0}), $$

where $\chi=\chi_{0}$ . Let

$$ \overline{\xi}_{S}\colon(X^{\{\!\!\!\ p\ \!\!\!\}}\times{\mathbb{S}})/_{\!\gamma_{p},\chi_{m}}{\mathbb{G}}_{m}\to{\mathbb{S}}/({\mathbb{G}}_{m}\ltimes_{\Ad_{\lambda}}G_{0}) $$

be the pre-composition of the latter with (6.5). Set $(\QCoh_{h})_{(X^{\{\!\!\!\ p\ \!\!\!\}}\times{\mathbb{S}})/_{\!\gamma_{p},\chi_{m}}{\mathbb{G}}_{m}}=\overline{\xi}_{\mathbb{S}}^{*}(({\mathcal{A}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\operatorname{\mathsf{-Mod}}})_{{\mathbb{S}}/({\mathbb{G}}_{m}\ltimes G_{0})})$ , where $({\mathcal{A}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\operatorname{\mathsf{-Mod}}})_{{\mathbb{S}}/({\mathbb{G}}_{m}\ltimes G_{0})}$ is constructed in Proposition 5.6. By construction, the pullback of $(\QCoh_{h})_{(X^{\{\!\!\!\ p\ \!\!\!\}}\times{\mathbb{S}})/_{\!\gamma_{p},\chi_{m}}{\mathbb{G}}_{m}}$ to $X^{\{\!\!\!\ p\ \!\!\!\}}\times{\mathbb{S}}$ is $\QCoh_{h}$ . Also, the category of global sections of $(\QCoh_{h})_{(X^{\{\!\!\!\ p\ \!\!\!\}}\times{\mathbb{S}})/_{\!\gamma_{p},\chi_{m}}{\mathbb{G}}_{m}}$ on $(X^{\{\!\!\!\ p\ \!\!\!\}}\times\{0\})/_{\!\gamma_{p}}{\mathbb{G}}_{m}$ is the category of quasi-coherent sheaves on $X/_{\!\gamma}{\mathbb{G}}_{m}$ .

### 6.3. Quantizations of $\QCoh(X)$ vs quantizations of ${\mathcal{O}}_{X}$

In this subsection we shall explain how, under a certain assumption, (6.8) below, $(\QCoh_{h})_{|X^{\{\!\!\!\ p\ \!\!\!\}}\times\hat{\mathbb{S}}}$ can be described as modules over a Frobenius-constant quantization of the algebra ${\mathcal{O}}_{X}$ . For the sake of simplicity we shall assume that $S$ is the spectrum of a field $k$ of characteristic $p>2$ and $X$ is a smooth $S$ -scheme.

For an integer $l\geq 0$ , set $G_{l}=\coker((\underline{A}_{h}^{*})^{\geq l-1}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\Ad}}{{\longrightarrow}}G)$ , where $(\underline{A}_{h}^{*})^{\geq l-1}\subset\underline{A}_{h}^{*}$ is the subgroup of elements equal to $1$ modulo $h^{l}$ . ## SUMMARY

Emerging research links the gut, skin, and oral microbiomes to allergies, with serine proteases (SPs) identified as potential allergens. This study leverages deep learning and pre-trained protein language models (pLMs) to uncover allergenic SPs in metagenomic data. First, we develop a model to identify the catalytic serine residue in serine hydrolases, demonstrating how pLMs capture structural information. Next, we create a deep learning framework to detect candidate SP allergens across gene catalogs, using the conserved catalytic triad to identify homologs in gut and oral sites despite low sequence identity. Our model predicts a putative SP allergen resembling V8 protease, a known trigger for protease-activated receptor 1. It also identifies a cysteine protease similar to Der f 1 from dust mites. Immunization with these proteases induced allergic responses, validating their allergenic potential experimentally. This approach uncovers candidate allergens beyond traditional methods, offering new targets for allergy research. A record of this paper’s transparent peer review process is included in the supplemental information.

## INTRODUCTION

The worldwide rise in allergic disease prevalence necessitates a deeper understanding of underlying mechanisms.1,2 Recent evidence suggests that the enzymatic activities of environmental allergens, including proteolytic activity, play a crucial role in initiating allergic responses at various tissue sites.3–5 Many immunodominant allergens can be categorized as serine or cysteine protease enzymes that follow a proteolytic mechanism defined by a catalytic triad in the active site.6–8 Despite disparate plant, animal, and fungal sources, these proteases share characteristics that suggest they have convergently evolved similar functions.9

This makes cysteine or serine protease activity a distinctive feature that could be exploited for allergen classification or discovery.10 The microbiome is one untapped source of possible allergenic proteases. While the gut microbiome and various microbial mechanisms have been implicated in the risk and devel-

opment of allergic diseases,11,12 further studies are needed to identify specific proteases involved in these pathways, including investigation of proteases, as these have previously been associated with allergic pathology.5

Aberrant protease reactions are a contributing factor in various inflammatory diseases.13 Many immunodominant allergens, such as the house dust mite allergen Der f 1 and the papaya allergen papain, are cysteine proteases, whose enzymatic functions are required for allergenic activity.5,14 Similarly, the proteolytic activity of serine proteases (SPs) can be linked to processes that initiate inflammation.15,16 SPs fall within the broader category of serine hydrolases (SHs), which collectively constitute ∼1% of the human genome and are present across the domains of life.17 Some microbes, such as Staphylococcus aureus, encode SPs that trigger an allergy-like response, leading to the production of SP-specific immunoglobulin E (IgE) and memory T helper 2 (Th2) cells.18 One mechanism of action involves SPs

proteolytically cleaving Mas-related G protein-coupled receptors (Mrgprs) and protease-activated receptors (PAR1/PAR2). This, in addition to other possible pathways, can activate sensory nociceptors, leading to itch, Th2-skewing dendritic cell (DC) migration, Th2 development, and Th2 recruitment.19–27 Microbial SPs have also been shown to act as itch triggers by activating PAR1, but whether they induce allergic disease is unknown.27 Other PARs are also activated by microbial proteases. Notably, PAR2 is targeted in lung tissue by Streptococcus pneumoniae28 and in Crohn’s disease by several microbes.29 PAR2 has been implicated in pain pathways in patients with irritable bowel syndrome30 and may contribute to nerve ending exposure through the dysregulation of tight junctions in the colonic epithelia.31 The diverse mechanisms by which SPs contribute to inflammatory processes, particularly in allergy-like responses, warrant further investigation. Several allergen prediction tools have been developed, each focusing on different methodologies to uncover sequences and some potential structural homologies with known allergens. AllergenFP32 utilizes E-descriptors to capture structural properties of all allergens, while AllerHunter33 employs the Smith- Waterman algorithm and BLOSUM62 matrices to train a machine learning model. Other tools, like AlgPred 2.0,34 rely on BLAST35-based similarity searches combined with multiple sequence alignments. By contrast, AllerCatPro 2.036 incorporates additional 3D structure information for epitope mapping but on a limited set of structures. Recent advancements in deep learning methods demonstrated an impressive ability to scale and capture evolutionary and structural features of proteins.37–42 Advanced structural homology search tools like Foldseek43 and DALI44 further aid in incorporating new information for functional annotation. For the prediction of allergens, ProAll-D45 uses a long short-term memory model. Other deep learning allergen prediction tools like ALLERDET46 and DeepAlgPro47 use custom-built deep learning models to predict allergens. Protein language models (pLMs) have been at the forefront of these advancements, demonstrating their ability to discern recurrent patterns across vast datasets of protein sequences.40,48–51 The success of pLMs in downstream transfer learning tasks across diverse biological topics, such as T cell receptor (TCR) epitope binding,52,53 protein-protein binding,54,55 remote homology,48 drug and protein interactivity,56 protein solubility,57 and secondary structure prediction,40,58 highlights their potential for the identification of allergens. Indeed, AllerTrans59 leverages pLMs for broad allergen prediction. Despite the advancements in prediction tools, structural similarity does not necessarily equate to functional similarity, and none of the aforementioned tools specifically investigate SP allergens, in which proteolytic function, rather than structure, imparts allergenicity. We hypothesize that the per-residue granularity of pLMs60,61 makes them well-suited to capture the highly conserved residues of an SP catalytic triad and that the transfer learning framework can be used to identify SPs with allergenic potential, using pLM embedding representations of annotated SPs as input data in the classifier. Traditional classification relies on clearly defined negative and positive classes, which are often difficult to establish in real-world scenarios.62 Creating a set of ‘‘negative’’ or non-

allergenic SPs can be challenging, as the set of known SPs not previously annotated as allergens may nevertheless include allergens, given the lack of systematic experimental screens of SPs for allergenic activity in the literature. Therefore, to identify SP allergens amidst other SPs and SHs, we employed a variation of positive unlabeled (PU) learning63 in which the set of unannotated SPs is weighted less heavily during training than known SP allergens, reflecting their uncertain allergenic status. PU learning has previously been used to address this same problem in the context of training machine learning models to predict disease genes62 and has been effectively implemented using machine learning algorithms like support vector machines (SVMs).64 In this context, SVMs optimize for the positive class while adjusting slack variables to handle outliers or negative examples.62 The successful application of deep learning to PU learning in fault detection65 further motivates the application of this methodology to SP allergen classification. To detect potential SP allergens, we employed two complementary strategies. First, we used pLM embeddings to train our models. Second, we explored the strengths of different modeling frameworks by training both a traditional SVM classifier and a deep learning model. We evaluated the generalizability of our models by applying them to microbial gene catalogs from diverse taxonomic groups, including the Unified Human Gastrointestinal Genome (UHGG)66,67 and Human Oral68 microbiome datasets from MGnify. Using the diverse Foldseek clustered AlphaFold Protein Structure Database (AFDB Clusters),69 we incorporated detailed knowledge of SP properties into our model. Our model predicted several thousand putative SP and even cysteine protease allergens in the gut and oral microbiomes. Among these, we pursued two specific candidates for experimental validation that showed structural similarity to the known allergen proteases, V8 protease and Der f 1. Using murine immunization models, we showed that these predicted SP and cysteine proteases are bona fide allergens based on their ability to activate an allergic immune response, characterized by Th2- skewing DC migration to draining lymph nodes and Th2 differentiation. Together, these approaches provide evidence that our classifier is able to predict SP-like allergens in large metagenomics datasets.

## RESULTS

Catalytic serine recognition using pLMs The highly conserved SH enzyme family is defined by a unique structural feature consisting of three amino acid residues that comprise a catalytic triad. Common motifs around the catalytic serine include GxSxG in lipases,70 SXXK in β-lactamases,71 and others. We aimed to assess how well pLM embeddings capture catalytic SP activity with allergenic potential. Using a logistic regression (LR) classifier trained on residue embeddings from pLMs, we investigated whether these embeddings could accurately identify catalytic serines within SH sequences. Three state-of-the-art pLMs—ESM-2,40 ProtT5,49 and ProSE51— were used to generate protein embeddings. We manually curated a set of 232 SH sequences and used a random split of catalytic and non-catalytic serines to train and evaluate the LR classifier. Given that the embedding dimensions vary

To benchmark the ability of each pLM to distinguish catalytic serines from non-catalytic serines in SH sequences, we used three metrics to compare the LR models trained on the pLM embeddings on a held-out test set (25%). First, we evaluated the area under the curve (AUC) of a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) plot (AUROC), in which each model’s true positive rate for identifying catalytic serines was plotted against its false positive rate. The performance of all three models was greater than 0.99 (Figure 1A). Second, we computed precision (the accuracy of each model’s positive predictions) and recall (the extent to which each model could capture all positive cases in the dataset) at different thresholds for each LR model. Of the three models, ESM-2 maintained maximum precision up to the highest recall value, beyond which its precision fell and continued to fall as recall increased further. Meanwhile, the precision of ProtT5 initially decreased at a lower recall value but remained relatively constant as recall increased further (Figure 1B). Third, to compute a quantitative value, we used the F1 score, which is the harmonic mean of the precision and recall values. All three pLMs had an F1 score above 0.94 (Figure 1C), ranging from 0.942 (ProSE) to 0.949 (ProtT5). The LR models trained on the ProSE, ProtT5, and ESM-2 pLM embeddings performed similarly on each of the benchmarking tasks for catalytic/non-catalytic classification. We next used principal-component analysis (PCA) to reduce the dimensionality of the embeddings of each of the catalytic and non-catalytic serines (Figure 1D). Catalytic serines clustered in each case. In the ProSE pLM, two distinct clusters appeared to catalog all

the catalytic serines. Not only were the two classes linearly separable in the embedding space, as shown by the accuracy of LR models, but they were also visually separable when the embeddings were projected onto the top two principal components. We chose to move forward with the ProtT5 embedding, which had the smallest embedding size (1,024), the highest F1 score, and comparable AUC and precision/recall to ESM-2. To examine whether specific features in the ProtT5 embedding could explain the LR model decision boundary, we analyzed the LR model using SHAP (Shapley additive explanations) values72,73 and found that no given embedding feature had an outsized impact on the model’s predictions (Figure S1).

Developing classification models for SP-like allergens We leveraged the Allergome database to identify 33 initial allergenic SPs (ASPs) from diverse taxonomies for use in our training data. We designated two negative classes for non-allergens: 116 non-allergenic serine proteases (NASPs) and 126 non-protease SHs (NPSHs). These initial proteases served as our foundational seeds—representative proteins used to collect additional training data. Collectively, we refer to all the proteins in the ASP, NASP, and NPSH sets as the SH class (STAR Methods). We utilized AFDB Clusters to supplement each initial seed in our training data with structurally similar proteins (Figure 2A). For each protein that mapped to a cluster, every cluster member was downloaded and used to augment the training dataset. This resulted in 9,004 members labeled as ‘‘allergens’’ and 80,841 members labeled as ‘‘non-allergens.’’ We included seeds from the Pfam protein families database74,75 (Pfam seeds, or PS) as additional non-allergen training examples. We developed two binary classification models to detect allergens: an SVM, representing a classical machine learning approach, and a multilayer perceptron (MLP), a deep learning feedforward neural network (Figure 2B). Our decision to employ binary classification models was driven by the complex nature of allergen detection in the embedding space. After clustering, each initial seed was augmented with more proteins based on structural clustering defined by AlphaFold Clusters.69 The allergenic SP class was then labeled as ‘‘allergen,’’ and the remaining classes and additional Pfam seeds were aggregated as ‘‘non-allergen.’’ (B) ProtT5 was run on every protein in each labeled class from the structural augmentation to generate embeddings. Two models were trained in parallel on a binary classification task to label proteins as allergens or non-allergens. One model was developed as an SVM, while the other followed a deep learning paradigm using an MLP neural network architecture. The neural network had two hidden layers of size 256 and 768 that ultimately mapped to the allergen or non-allergen classes. the entries in the NPSH class. The highest AUROC achieved on the test set was 98.5%. To find the optimal MLP model, we employed RayTune76 to optimize layer size, batch size, and class weights by randomly sampling hyperparameter values. We again split the ASP and NASP classes into 80/20 train/test sets, then further subdivided the original 20% test set, creating a validation set and a final test set that each comprised 10% of the ASP and NASP data. We then augmented the training set with all of the entries in the NPSH and PS classes. We trained each model for 20 epochs, calculating the AUROC of the validation set at 20% intervals within each epoch. Upon training completion, an AUROC evaluation was performed on the designated final test set, and the model that achieved the highest AUROC (95.6%) was chosen as the optimal model (Figures S2C and S2D). The MLP classifier consists of four layers: an input of 1,024 dimensions (ProtT5 embedding size), which is projected to 256 dimensions, then to 768 dimensions, and finally to 2 dimensions representing allergen and non-allergen (Figure 2B). Among the three approaches (MLP, SVM, and zero-shot classification models), the MLP demonstrated superior performance (Figures S2E and S2F), leading us to select it as our primary model for allergen discovery. When we first applied our MLP, trained on SH families, to the oral (791,924 proteins) and gut (4,601,771 proteins) catalogs, it labeled ∼10% of each catalog as allergens, likely an overestimate due to limited negative examples. To address this, we incorporated over one million Pfam seed proteins as additional nonallergen data, expanding coverage of diverse protein domains.

While most hits belonged to the Firmicutes and Actinobacteria phyla, the gut protein catalog uniquely contained hits from species within the Desulfobacterota and Verrucomicrobiota phyla (Figure 4B). Using a priority scoring metric we developed that aggregated query coverage, target coverage, alignment template modeling (TM) score, and sequence identity from Foldseek with the e value of any hit also found in the InterProScan results, we filtered (STAR Methods) our set of 3,874 gut and 658 oral proteins down to 412 gut (a 9-fold reduction) and 147 oral proteins (a 4-fold reduction) (Figures 4C and 4D). Observing a positive correlation between our priority score and Foldseek’s e value, we ranked our filtered set of proteins by −log(e value) from Foldseek. Thirteen oral allergens in the filtered set were predicted to be encoded by Prevotella species, including three of the top 15 proteases in the ranked list (Table S1), which aligns with Prevotella’s known involvement in oral inflammation80 and potential links to asthma.81 The gut gene catalog revealed 69 hits predicted to be encoded by Lachnospiraceae, including 6 of the top 25 microbial proteases (Table S2). Notably, Lachnospiraceae members have been implicated in early-life egg and milk allergies,82,83 hinting at a potential role of these gut proteases in allergic pathways. To evaluate the prevalence of these highly ranked predicted allergens in the human gut microbiome, we cross-referenced these proteins with a gut metagenomics collection of healthy individuals from the Framingham Heart Study (FHS).84 We detected 110 of the predicted gut allergens in the FHS gut microbiome gene catalog with high homology (sequence identity > 90%, query coverage > 93%). Of those, three proteins in different Lachnospiraceae species were highly prevalent in the FHS population: Roseburia hominis (77.2% prevalent), Eubacterium eligens (67% prevalent), and Eubacterium rectale (87% prevalent). All of these putative allergens contained a subtilase Pfam domain and showed high structural and sequence similarity to known subtilisin allergens (Figure S4). Both R. hominis and E. eligens have been associated with a general lowering of inflammation85,86; however, E. rectale was found to be enriched in pediatric patients with food or respiratory allergies.87

were discovered only by the MLP classifier and not by DIA- MOND.77 We focused on proteases with low sequence identity (15%–35%) to their closest Foldseek hit while maintaining high structural similarity (>0.7 TM score). As a result, we identified 52 gut and 45 oral putative proteases. We chose to structurally search these putative allergens against known crystal structures in the Protein Data Bank (PDB) and predicted structures in Swiss-Prot. We pursued two specific hits: one to a V8 protease from the gut protein catalog and another to a Der f 1 cysteine protease in the oral protein catalog. We chose these hits for their low sequence identity (in the ‘‘twilight zone’’88 of 20%–35%) and high structural homology (>0.8 TM score). The MLP model’s confidence in labeling these two sequences as allergenic was consistently high, even when we altered residues within, near, and far from the catalytic triad (Figure S5). Our first unknown allergen protease demonstrated high structural homology (TM score 0.87) and low sequence identity (31.05%) to an experimentally characterized crystal structure of a V8 protease from Staphylococcus aureus (Figure 5A, left). Sequence and structural alignment of the unknown allergen and the S. aureus V8 protease revealed complete conservation of the catalytic triad and overall high sequence and structural identity in the catalytic domain (Figure 5B, left). The putative enzyme is predicted to be from Staphylococcus schleiferi in the gut catalog. Using the Joint Genome Institute Integrated Microbial Genomes (JGI IMG) database, we identified several transporter proteins among the regulatory elements in the genomic neighborhood of the putative enzyme (Figure 5C, left). Consistent with this, the enzyme is predicted to contain a signal peptide. A sequence similarity search of the putative SP against other microbial genomes yielded hits mostly in the Firmicutes phylum (Figure 5D, left), many of which were from other Staphylococcus species. The identification of this putative V8 protease within the gut catalog highlights the potential to discover many uncharacterized SPs that may share similar allergenic functions along the PAR1 axis. The presence of cysteine proteases (CPs) among our predicted allergens is noteworthy given that our training data consisted solely of SPs, highlighting the MLP model’s ability to generalize beyond its initial scope. To validate the plausibility of CP hits, we focused on a putative CP allergen from Tannerella forsythia with high similarity to the allergen Der f 1 from the American house dust mite Dermatophagoides farinae. We found that the putative enzyme had high structural homology (TM score 0.87) and low sequence identity (25.71%) to Der f 1 (Figure 5A, right) and that the catalytic domain was highly similar, with perfect sequence and structural alignment of the catalytic triad (Figure 5B, right). The genomic neighborhood of the putative CP included a radical S-adenosyl-L-methionine (SAM) enzyme as well as transporter proteins (Figure 5C, right). We found homologous genes to this putative CP in a wider range of species than we did for the SP homologs (Figure 5D, right). In a separate sequence similarity search, we found a sequence with 99% similarity to the putative CP in a Dialister invisus genome recovered from metagenomic sequencing of stool samples from the FHS, in which D. invisus is prevalent (>85%) despite typically being found in the oral cavity.91 The presence of a Der f 1-like CP in the gut, originating from an oral microbe also known to colonize the gut,92 raises the possibility that allergic responses to this putative allergen could involve both the oral and gut environments.

## DISCUSSION

This study describes a deep learning framework using pLMs and AFDB Clusters to enhance identification of allergenic proteases in metagenomic datasets. Our approach successfully catalogs and predicts different putative allergenic proteases from gut and oral metagenomes. The conservation of the catalytic triad in typical SPs, shaped by convergent evolution,9,95 makes it an ideal target for deep learning and structural approaches. We demonstrated 99% accuracy of three state-of-the-art pLMs in distinguishing catalytic from non-catalytic serines. Encouraged by pLMs’ ability to identify catalytic triads in SHs, we hypothesized they could predict SP allergenicity. To address difficulties verifying negative examples, we trained our model to prioritize known allergens, penalizing negatives at varying rates. We expanded training data 10- to 100-fold using AFDB Clusters, incorporating SPs with low sequence homology but similar structure and putative function. This strategy proved effective, with our MLP classifier achieving an AUROC of 0.95, accurately

distinguishing subtle differences between allergenic and nonallergenic SPs. When applied to large oral and gut microbiome protein catalogs, our model initially overpredicted allergens, likely due to overfitting on the small set of known allergenic proteases. This was rectified by retraining with over a million Pfam seed proteins, a step that served as a powerful regularizer. By including this vast negative set, we compelled the model to learn a simpler, more biologically meaningful decision boundary, forcing it to discard spurious correlations and instead identify the core features most predictive of allergenic function. This provided a broader proteome view, which elevated the model’s performance in discriminating allergenic and non-allergenic proteases. While these findings highlight the prevalence of predicted allergenic proteases in common gut taxa (e.g., Lachnospiraceae species), their presence alone does not confirm allergenicity. Using proteases predicted to be allergic or non-allergic, we validated their predicted allergic capability experimentally. This suggests that our model can be used in larger-scale efforts to determine an allergic risk score associated with colonization with microbial taxa. However, associations of certain taxa with allergies or immune-mediated effects underscore the complexity of microbial-host interactions. Additional work will need to be performed to validate the specific role of microbial proteases in promoting allergic disease. Many predicted allergens belonged to the subtilase family, possibly reflecting its size as the second-largest SP family across life domains.96,97 While 48% of our initial ASP training seeds were from this family (potentially causing bias), several subtilisins are known allergens, and research links human leukocyte antigen (HLA)-DQ genotype to subtilisin hypersensitivity.98

Our MLP model transcended primary sequence limitations, identifying critical functional motifs even within the lower sequence identity. It successfully flagged putative SP allergens sharing conserved catalytic triads with structural matches despite low pairwise identity. The model detected CPs despite their absence in training data, showcasing the model’s ability to learn essential protein features. Experimental evaluation confirmed that two putative allergenic proteases directly promoted allergic immune responses dependent on their functional activity. EXPERIMENTAL MODEL AND STUDY PARTICIPANT DETAILS

METHOD DETAILS

Materials Availability There are restrictions to the availability of the Serine Protease and Cysteine Protease used in the study because we had them both expressed and purified from a third-party vendor, Genscript, and used the entire aliquot in the above mentioned experiments.

Catalytic Serine Classification in SHs Every SH sequence was collected from the 232 SHs in a previous study.108 Each sequence was passed through the three protein language models (pLMs) ESM-2,40 ProSE51 and ProtT549 and embeddings were generated on a per-residue basis. All of the serine embeddings were collected in every sequence and labeled as ‘catalytic’ or ‘non-catalytic’ using the information stored in UniProt.109

To ensure deterministic results, we trained a logistic regression model using the LogisticRegression model from the sklearn.linear_model library101 with the random_state parameter set to 0. To address the class imbalance between the number of catalytic and non-catalytic serines, we employed the SMOTE (synthetic minority over-sampling technique)102 to create additional examples from the catalytic class, thus enhancing classification performance. After splitting the dataset into 75% for training and 25% for testing (test_train_split in sklearn.model_selection) the precision/recall and ROC curves were calculated (roc_curve, precision_recall_curve in sklearn.metrics). The F1-score was calculated on each of the held out test datasets for every pLM example as well (f1_score in sklearn.metrics). We used principal component analysis (PCA) for the dimensionality reduction to evaluate the embeddings from the different classes (pca in sklearn.decomposition). We displayed the first and second principal components (PC) and the explained variance for each PC. Each plot was rendered in GraphPad Prism version 10.1.1 (270).

Catalytic Serine model explainability analysis To delve into the decision-making process of our catalytic serine model, we employed SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) values72,73 to interpret the model’s reliance on specific features within ProtT5 embeddings. Specifically, we utilized the LinearExplainer module to analyze the contribution of each index value within the embeddings to the model’s predictions. To visualize these contributions, we generated force plots, highlighting the embedding features that exerted the most influence on the model’s output. We used the summary_plot function to visualize the specific contributions made by each feature.

Constructing a Serine Protease Allergen Set A total of 33 allergenic serine protease (ASP) positives were downloaded from Allergome (www.allergome.com).110,111 The search query ‘‘serine protease’’ was used to filter specifically for SPs within the broader allergen database. The corresponding UniProt accession numbers109 were then used to download the protein sequences of these allergens. To compile a set of likely negative non-allergenic serine proteases (NASP), we constructed a query in Swiss-Prot112 to identify bacterial proteins that were classified as serine proteases (keyword:KW-0720) but lacked evidence of allergenic activity. We restricted the query to bacterial proteases (taxonomy_name:2) smaller than 800 amino acids (length:[* TO 800]) that were not tagged as

Expanding Training Data with AFDB Clusters To enrich the training data, each of the three groups was augmented with additional sequences retrieved using the Foldseek clustered AlphaFold database (AFDB Clusters).69 The Foldseek cluster algorithm applies both sequence and structural homology to group proteins into clusters. Then, within each cluster, only sequences associated with the ‘‘AFDB/Foldseek’’ clustering step were downloaded and incorporated into the augmented training set. Utilizing AFDB cluster augmentation, the ASP, NASP, and NPSH sets were each expanded. The ASP set was increased to a total of 8,685 sequences, the NASP set to 20,708 sequences, and the NPSH set to 59,165 sequences.

We generate a random split of the dataset into a training set A⊂{1;…;n}, which contains ASPs, NASPs, and NPSHs, and a validation set B⊂{1;…;n}, which only contains ASPs and NASPs, i.e. if i ϵ B, yi ϵ {ASP;NASP}. We use the first subset A to train a weighted support vector machine with the aim of discriminating the positive class ASP from the negative classes NASP and NPSH. Recognizing that the negative class containing the hardest classification examples is NASP (as it consists of only SPs), the hyperparameters are tuned on the classification accuracy in a validation set B comprising only ASPs and NASPs. The model is defined as follows. Let ϕ : ℝ1024→ℝd be a given feature map, which translates the input x into a feature vector ϕ(x); in the simplest version of the model, we can take the identity ϕ(x) = x. The support vector machine discriminates positives from true negatives through a score function f(x) = ϕ(x)Tβ which is linear in the features, i.e.f(x) > 0 indicates that an example with input x is positive. The parameter β is estimated through the following optimization:

Multilayer perceptron neural network A limitation of the support vector machine is that the score function f(x) is linear in the feature vector ϕ(x), which is fixed up to the scaling factor σ. We thus fit a more flexible neural network classifier with a similar strategy of weighting each term in the loss according to the class yi of the sample. Let ψθ : ℝ1024→ℝd be a multilayer perceptron (MLP) with two hidden layers and parameters θ.104 We fit a classifier by minimizing the weighted cross-entropy objective:

minimize ∑

i ∈A

wyi log ( 1 + exp ( − ρ(yi)ψθ(xi)Tβ )) subject to θ; β (Equation 3)

As before, the hyperparameters wASP; wNASP; wNPSH > 0 are learned by cross-validation on a validation set B containing only ASPs and NASPs. We additionally train the hyperparameter for Pfam seeds (PS), wPS > 0 in order to expose the classifier to a larger distribution of training data. Note that the objectives for the support vector machine and the neural network model are very similar. The former uses a hinge loss instead of a binary cross-entropy or logistic loss, and includes a penalty term λ‖β‖2. However, the main difference is that in this case we are learning a complex non-linear feature map ψθ instead of using the one-parameter feature map ϕ of the Gaussian kernel. The MLP architecture has three overall layers with two hidden layers. The fixed size input vectors of 1024 dimensions from ProtT5 embeddings are projected to 768 dimensions then to 1536 dimensions to a final classification output layer of 1, representing the classification of SP allergen versus non-allergen. We implemented this model using Pytorch Lightning105 to create a classifier that included all of the training, validation, and testing steps. Each embedding from the ASP, NASP, NPSH and PS classes was weighted differently, utilizing the PyTorch104 Binary Cross Entropy with Logits Loss function with the weights specified as a hyperparameter. We used a leaky rectified linear unit (ReLU)115 with dropout regularization and a weight decay in our AdamW optimizer.116

Hyperparameter optimization and training To optimize our binary SP classification neural network’s performance, we used RayTune,76 a hyperparameter tuning library. We conducted a randomized grid search, evaluating 20 models concurrently with diverse hyperparameter combinations selected by RayTune (Table S5). Each model was trained for 200 epochs using the Async Successive Halving (ASHA) scheduler,117 which facilitates early stopping by terminating models based on minimizing training loss. After each epoch, we monitored validation accuracy, AUROC, and F1 score (from the sklearn.metrics version 1.4.0 library), with testing accuracy assessed after complete training. For training purposes we randomly split the ASP and NASP classes into 80% training, 10% validation and 10% test using the random_split function from PyTorch with a fixed generator to ensure reproducibility. We added all the Pfam seeds and NPSH enzymes to the training set. We picked the best performing model, which had the hyperparameters:

Layer 1 Size: 256, Layer 2 Size: 768 Learning Rate: 1.4e-4, Batch Size: 128, Allergenic SP Weight: 6, Non-Allergenic SP Weight: 1, Serine Hydrolase Weight: 2, Pfam Seeds Weight: 1, Dropout Probability: 24.696%

With that model, we trained the classifier on 20 epochs with validation occurring every 20% of the training and a final test accuracy assessment after completion.

## Preserving Information in Quantum Systems via Coherent Driving

Abstract

Among the fundamental phenomena that characterize a quantum system is coherent superposition between states, which we can write for a two-level system as:

|ψ⟩= α|0⟩+ eiφβ|1⟩. (1)

A superposition is characterized by a phase φ which can be difficult to conceptualize with our physical intuition, trained only by experience in a classical world. Perhaps we can best approach it by considering the phase of classical waves, which we can concretely visualize, andwhichleadtosomeanalogousphenomenalikeinterference. Ineffectthere is additional information in the system beyond the probability that it is measured in one state vs. the other. Thisphaseis botha resourceand avulnerability of quantum systems. On one hand, it gives the system another degree of freedom which we can control. On the other hand, it can be easily lost, since the phase of a superposition tends to be very sensitive to fluctuations in the system’s surrounding environment. The length of time that the phase remains known in a system (or equivalently, that the system maintains its information) is called the coherence time. In this thesis I will discuss two examples in which a coherent superposition of states is used to preserve information in a quantum system. In both cases the key laboratory tool used to access the quantum system is an AC field of classical amplitude which coherently drives the states, and in both cases we will see the beneficial properties of the stationary solutions of the combined system plus field, which are superposition states (in the basis that does not include the field). Chapter 1 will deal with an example of a coherent field extending the coherence time of a two-level system. I will show experimental data demonstrating this effect in the electron spin of the silicon vacancy in diamond, where the coherent driving field is a strain field in the carbon lattice. Chapter 2 will explain how the decay channels of a single atomic system can be controlled using superpositions of states, a phenomena which could be used to increase the fidelity of a state measurement. These results are computational rather than experimental, but I will suggest a real quantum system in which this phenomena could be demonstrated and calculate expected results.

### 1.1 Introduction

Thenegatively-chargedsiliconvacancy(SiV)centerindiamondcomprisesasiliconatom

located interstitially between two vacancies in the carbon lattice. By defining a qubit

on its ground state electron spin levels, which are coherent at cryogenic temperature, it

can be used to store quantum information. It has the additional benefits of stability in

nanostructures, and optical transitions which allow its state to be optically initialized

and read out. Of particular interest to this dissertation, however, is the uniquely high

strain response (1 PHz/strain) of the SiV’s optical and orbital energy levels2,3. Because

of spin-orbit coupling the qubit spin states have an orbital characteristic, so in the pres-

ence of an off-axis magnetic field, they also couple to strain. Static strain fields can be

used to tune the energy states of the SiV, which is especially useful for the optical tun-

ing because the SiV is first-order insensitive to electric Stark tuning which is commonly

used in related defects3. Alternatively, an oscillating strain field can be used to reso-

nantely and coherently drive the SiV’s spin with impressively large strain response of

∼100 THz/strain2,4. (We note that oscillation strain fields resonant with the spin tran-

sition can also have off-resonant effects on the orbital and optical states (see sections 1.7

and 1.5.1)). The potential for large couplings between SiV spins and coherent phonons

holds great promise for exploring the emerging field of quantum phononics.

The phonon is an intriguing up-and-coming candidate as a quantum information

carrier in on-chip quantum communications. It holds several distinct advantages over

its electromagnetic cousin the photon:

• Because the speed of sound is ∼4-5 orders of magnitude slower than the speed of

light, a phonon has a much shorter wavelength than a photon of the same fre-

quency, enabling smaller device footprints and many more devices on a chip.

2


<!-- Page 25 -->


• Light readily couples to the vacuum, limiting the extent to which it can be con-

fined in a photonic device. Sound, on the other hand, has a greatly suppressed

coupling to the vacuum, allowing greater confinement in phononic structures.

This has enabled phononic cavity architectures reaching quality factors on the

order of 1e95,6

• Phonons couple to many different kinds of quantum systems7,8, allowing them

to serve as an intermediary between solid state defects, superconducting qubits

and photons via optomechanical interactions.

Phononic quantumnetworkshavebeenproposedin which quantum states are encoded

in long-lived electronic spins and can then be converted into propagating phonon wave

packets and reabsorbed efficiently by a distant spin memory9,10. Realizing a quantum

state transfer that is mediated by phonons requires strong single spin–phonon cou-

pling10, typically achieved in high-quality-factor phononic resonators7,9,8. To suppress

thedecoherenceofthespinsduetomagneticfieldnoiseandneighboringnuclearspins11,

dynamical decoupling pulse sequences are often applied to preserve the spin coherence

by periodically refocusing the phase of the spin state. However, a major challenge arises

when spins are embedded within resonant phononic cavities, in which the continuous

couplingbetweenthespinsandthephononicmodescanconflictwithpulseddynamical

decoupling protocols that require precise spin control pulse sequences interlaced with

periods of free evolution.

An alternative scheme to mitigate the decoherence is to use a continuous-wave dy-

namical decoupling protocol, in which a coherent field is continuously applied and the

quantum information is encoded in the dressed states defined by the interaction of the

driving field with the spins12. This continuous dressing field decouples the spin from

demonstratedwithNVcentersindiamond13,14,15, divacancycentersinSiC16, semicon-

ductor donor spin qubits17 and trapped ions18. Because the energy splitting between

1.2 Surface acoustic wave device

We choose surface acoustic waves (SAW) as our mechanical driving modes because we

can transduce them piezoelectrically and because of their large strain amplitudes and

good mode confinement close to the diamond surface. A 1.4 μm layer of aluminum ni-

tride (AlN) is sputtered onto a bulk electronic grade diamond to piezoelectrically tran-

duce the SAW modes. Metal interdigital transducers (IDTs) are patterned on top and

designed to launch a beam with a two-dimensional Gaussian profile in order to focus

the acoustic energy to a waist of about two wavelength. The confinement in the third

dimension is inherently provided by the surface confinement of the SAW, as shown in

the simulated strain profile in Fig. 1.1(a). The SiVs are generated around 100 nm below

the AlN and diamond interface by implantation of silicon ions. We control the implan-

tation density to make sure that the SiVs are sparse enough that they can be individually

addressed with a resonant laser.

The two IDTs have a combined bandwidth of ∼100 MHz, as measured in the S-

parameter characterization in Fig. 1.1(b). The total transmission loss from the whole

SAW measurement path (measured at the fridge input and output ports) is -37dB at the

peak frequency of 3.35GHz. The loss comes from the device impedance mismatch, ma-

terial loss, bulk scattering and cable and wirebonding loss. The estimated SAW powers

We see that the dressed states and the bare states are coupled by the same polariza-

As the amplitude of the dressing SAW increases, the associated periodic strain mod-

1.5.1 AC Stark shift

Both the optical and the orbital levels of the SiV are modulated by strain fields with an

amplitude of ∼1 PHz/strain2, so an AC Stark shift could result from either. Given the

SiV spin-strain susceptibility of ∼100THz/strain2, we expect that the strain amplitude

at the SiV location due to a dressing SAW field with Rabi frequency of 320 MHz is

approximately 3e-6. We calculate that the optical AC Stark shift arising from this SAW

field is Ω2 opt/Δopt, which is on the order of tens of kHz, and the orbital AC Stark shift

arising from this SAW field is equivalently Ω2 orb/Δorb, which is on the order of hundreds

of MHz. Thus the optical AC Stark shift is likely a negligible effect, while the orbital AC

Start shift may significantly contribute to this effect because the orbital levels are much

closer in energy to the SAW frequency than the optical levels.

The extended coherence time of the dressed states may be limited by the coupling be-

spin qubit protocol may apply better to the SnV spin because of the larger frequency

difference between the spin splitting and orbital splitting, though its SAW-spin suscep-

tibility has yet to be experimentally demonstrated. Finally, this noise mechanism could

be suppressed by engineering the surrounding phonon density states to suppress the or-

bital state decay pathways. This has been demonstrated in the past to extend the ground

state orbital lifetime of the SiV23.

### 2.1 Introduction

Optical cycling transitions are an important feature of atomic systems, allowing high-

fidelity state measurement in solid-state quantum defects34,35,36,11, as well as trapped

ions and atoms37,38,39. Cycling transitions are additionally used to cool and trap atoms

and ions40,41,42,43. Deviation from ideal cyclicity due to additional spurious decay chan-

nels decreases the fidelity of state readout44,34 and reduces the efficiency of cooling and

trapping. The pursuit of improved cyclicity in optical transitions has lead to recent

advances in molecular design45,46,47,48 and demonstrations of selective cavity enhance-

ment of optical transitions36,49. This relies, however, on the cavity linewidth being nar-

rower than the spectral separation between the desired decay paths and the undesired

decay paths, which may be technologically infeasible. This chapter will discuss another

means of increasing cyclicity, which leverages the coherent interference of decay paths,

controlled via externally applied driving fields.

The phenomenon of coherent interference of decay has been proposed for tailor-

ing of spectral lineshapes50,51, population inversion for lasing purposes52, and squeez-

ing51. It is closely related to coherent population trapping53, though coherent popula-

tion trapping is usually framed in terms of a dark superposition state which cannot be

populated by an applied field, whereas interference of decay involves a dark superposi-

tion state which does not spontaneously decay.

This chapter will focus on the relative enhancement and suppression of different

decay paths to increase the cyclicity of a given transition, rather than suppression of all

decay, as has been emphasized in past investigations. We will focus on how interference

of decay can be applied to cycling transitions and we will describe the conditions under

which atomic systems would display an increase in cyclicity. We will additionally give

2.6 Strong drive model intuition

Let us now examine the intuition for the TDM constraints seen in Sections 2.4 and

2.5. The first-order requirement for the strong-driving scheme to work is that the po-

larization of μe1g2 and μe2g2 must be parallel. This is necessary in order for the decay path

from |e1⟩to |g2⟩to experience full interference with the decay path from |e2⟩to |g2⟩. This

constraint is relaxed in the case where more than two excited states are involved in the de-

structiveinterference ofdecay, for thesame reason that three vectorsin two-dimensional

space can sum to zero even if none of them are parallel with either of the others. Systems

with three or more excited states are beyond the purview of this dissertation.

Second,theexcitedstatesmustbeclosetogether,relativetotheopticaldrivingstrength

(Fig. 2.3(a)). This constrains the maximum excited state splitting ωess, given the realistic

optical Rabi rates that can be achieved.

Third, we wish to avoid spurious excitation from |g2⟩. That is, the large optical field

that couples |g1⟩to |e1⟩and |e2⟩should ideally not create any coupling between |g2⟩and

the excited states. In order to preserve the fidelity of the measurement distinguishing

between the ground states, |g2⟩should be completely dark under the application of the

optical readout fields. This is the case if the driving field is off-resonant from the transi-

Δg2e1, Δg2e2 ≫ΩS (2.5)

### 2.10 Discussion

We have proposed and analyzed two methods for enhancing the cyclicity of optical tran-

sitions in atomic systems by exploiting the coherent interference of decay paths. The

first, a strong-drive scheme, relies on a certain phase and amplitude relationship between

the bare state transition dipole moments. Under these conditions, a single strong driv-

ing field will effectively drive the system between a ground state and an excited state

superposition that decays only to that ground state. Using the negatively charged nickel

vacancy center in diamond as a concrete example, we demonstrated that this approach

can enable high-fidelity optical readout even under misaligned magnetic fields, where

inherent cycling transitions do not exist.

The second method, the auxiliary-drive scheme, requires an additional metastable

statecoupledtotheexcitedstatemanifold,whichallowsfine-tunedcontrolofthedressed-

state composition via the amplitude and detuning of an auxiliary field. This approach

relaxes the stringent requirements on transition dipole moments and drive strength im-

posed by the strong-drive scheme, while maintaining the ability to coherently suppress

undesired decay channels. Simulations show that appropriate tuning of the auxiliary

field can sustain continuous photon cycling and high emission counts at moderate op-

tical powers.

53


<!-- Page 76 -->


Together, these methods provide a general framework for engineering effective cy-

cling transitions in a wide range of atomic and solid-state systems, including color cen-

ters, trapped ions, and molecular emitters. By leveraging quantum interference in the

decay process, they circumvent the need for narrow optical cavities or highly selective

transitions, offering a scalable route to improved optical readout fidelity in quantum

technologies.

In this dissertation we have seen two examples of the marvelous power of quantum

superpositions. In Chapter 1 we demonstrated that a quantum superposition of two

spin states is less sensitive to noise than the original bare spin states. This extends the

coherence time of the system, allowing it to retain its quantum information for longer.

transition, maintaining the information of the system’s initial state for a longer period

of time and increasing the fidelity of a state readout measurement.

# Increased cyclicity of atomic transitions via coherent interference of decay paths

**Authors:** Eliza Cornell Affiliation: John A. Paulson School for Engineering and Applied Sciences, Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA Benjamin Pingault Affiliation: Pritzker School of Molecular Engineering and Chicago Quantum Institute, University of Chicago, Chicago, Illinois, USA Affiliation: Q-NEXT and Materials Science Division, Argonne National Laboratory, Lemont, Illinois, USA Gergő Thiering Affiliation: HUN-REN Wigner Research Centre for Physics, P.O.
